title: Field Compass: Competitive Scenarios vs LLM API Providers
executive_summary: A lightweight, scenario-driven reference for sellers and AE engineers to quickly map buyer signals to Redwood positioning versus common LLM API provider archetypes. Not a full battlecard — this is a rapid decision compass for live calls and discovery. Contains three competitor archetypes, typical traps customers fall into, top objections and concise rebuttals, and quick scripts for discovery and close.
audience: AEs, solutions engineers, SDRs prepping for inbound product/tech meetings, and field enablement leads.
compass_framework: Use three axes to orient: 1) Economics (per-token, embeddings, inference unit economics), 2) Reliability (SLOs, fallbacks, availability under surge), 3) Integration friction (auth, schema/tooling, private deployments). Score a competitor along these axes during discovery to land the right message.
competitor_archetypes: Model-First Provider: high publicity on model quality, frequent new model drops, limited ops controls. Strengths: latest model features, strong research PR. Weaknesses: unpredictable latency/cost at scale, lightweight enterprise controls. Field traps: buyers conflate headline model improvements with production fit. Rebuttal hooks: emphasize serving economics and predictable SLAs; ask about latency SLOs and cost targets for 100k requests/day.

Cloud Endpoint Vendor: managed endpoints on cloud infra, easy to start, integrated with cloud billing. Strengths: one-stop cloud integration, enterprise support. Weaknesses: limited batching/quantization options, region lock-in risks. Field traps: buyers assume cloud vendor equals cheaper or easier at scale. Rebuttal hooks: surface dedicated capacity and private deployment options; ask about multi-region failover and unit cost at peak concurrency.

Open-Source Runtime / Self-Host Stack: low sticker cost, high control, heavy ops lift. Strengths: flexibility, raw cost upside. Weaknesses: operational overhead, hidden reliability gaps, team distraction. Field traps: engineering teams underestimate SRE time and model compatibility issues. Rebuttal hooks: bring up predictable throughput guarantees, KV-cache/auto-batching benefits, and our managed fallback policies for graceful degradation.
scenario_quadrants: Drift Scenario (model churn risk): Customer uses multiple new models and fears lock-in. Message: Redwood lets you pin model versions and route by policy; you get model experimentation without surfacing runtime regressions to users.

Squeeze Scenario (cost vs latency): Customer needs sub-200ms tail latencies at 50 RPS and is price-sensitive. Message: highlight intelligent batching, caching, and quantization recommendations from Redwood Optimize plus Dedicated pools for predictable latency.

Blackout Scenario (region/capacity outage): Customer needs failover guarantees across regions. Message: show smart routing + automatic model fallbacks and Dedicated burst capacity to preserve critical flows under outages.

Migration Scenario (legacy self-host to managed): Customer skeptical of moving to hosted. Message: outline stepwise migration path: start with routing policy for non-sensitive traffic, run audits, then pilot Dedicated or Private deployments with traffic mirroring.
top_objections_and_rebuttals: Objection: 'Your per-token price is higher than provider X' -> Rebuttal: Break down total cost of ownership: tokens + tail latencies + engineering time. Ask: what is your tokens/day and peak concurrency? Offer a modeled comparison using their telemetry and Redwood Optimize suggestions.

Objection: 'We can self-host for cheaper' -> Rebuttal: quantify hidden costs (SRE headcount, time to recover, model compatibility work). Offer case example: mid-market fintech saved 0.75 FTE of ops time/month and avoided 3 incident rollbacks in first quarter by using Dedicated capacity.

Objection: 'We need latest model features, vendor Y always drops new models first' -> Rebuttal: agree on importance of model innovation, then pivot to serving risk: ask how they validate regressions and rollback on regressions. Position Redwood’s model catalog + transparent performance profiles and easy rollbacks as safe experimentation surface.

Objection: 'We need VPC/on-prem for compliance' -> Rebuttal: explain Private offering, customer-managed control plane, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit logs. Offer an SOW template and security check-list to move conversation forward.

Objection: 'What happens during big surges?' -> Rebuttal: explain Dedicated autoscaling policies, burst pools, and graceful fallback to cheaper model variants or cross-region routing; show latency & cost degradation charts from prior incidents (anonymized).
field_scripts: Discovery opener: 'Tell me about a recent time your LLM endpoint missed SLA or surprised you on cost—what happened and how did you triage?' (goal: surface pain on tail latencies, burst behavior, and lack of observability).
Integration probe: 'How do you manage secrets, model version pins, and environment parity between staging and prod today?' (goal: find friction for Private/Dedicated sell).

Close nudge: 'If we could give you a predictable per-token model with canary rollouts and audited KMS integration in 8 weeks, what needs to happen internally to say yes?' (goal: map internal stakeholders and redlines).
data_points_and_benchmarks: Suggested bench: 99th percentile token latency targets for chat flows: < 250ms for Dedicated use-cases, < 400ms for hosted API under typical burst. Use these as conversation anchors.
Suggested cost anchor: present an example where batching + KV-caching reduced per-token compute by 35% on a 2M token/month workload compared to naive endpoint usage.
Reliability anchor: cite Dedicated SLA: 99.9% uptime with documented fallback policies (use as conversational differentiator).
